newsitem.title: FRANCE: French tax hikes add limited cost on companies.
newsitem.headline: French tax hikes add limited cost on companies.

text.p: The French government's imposition of higher taxes on companies will dent profits slightly in the short term but is not seen having a lasting negative impact on corporate performance, analysts and industry sources said on Monday.

"Our feeling here is that there will be a limited immediate impact on company profits. But at the same time it shows the government is comitted to EMU which is good for the (share) market," said Gary Dugan, market strategist at JP Morgan in London.
"The government aims to raise 22 billion francs ($3.6 billion) with the tax increase, that's some two to three percent of the total profits of CAC-40 companies," he added.
Hugues de Montvallon, analyst at brokers Oddo, saw a more pronounced impact and expected French shares to be four to five percent lower as a result of the tax increase.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn announced two measures aimed at getting more revenues from the corporate sector to improve state finances in the run up to European economic and monetary union. The main measure was a additional 15 percent surcharge on the corporate tax rate for the years 1997 and 1998 after which this special increase will come down to 10 percent.
The basic corpoparate tax rate is currently 33.3 percent of taxable profits and since 1995 there has been a surcharge of 10 percent bringing the effective tax rate to 36.6 percent.

The extra surcharge of 15 percent of the basic tax rate, which will remain unchanged at 33.3 percent, will increase the surcharge to 25 percent and the effective tax rate for 1997 and 1998 to 41.6 percent. In 1999 and thereafter the effective rate will come down to 39.9 percent.

The other change announced by Strauss-Kahn concerns capital gains. These will no longer be taxed at 19 percent but the gains will be added to the total taxable profit and then taxed at the 41.6 percent rate.
The tax rises will apply to companies with more than 50 million francs in annual turnover.
French companies were reluctant to comment on the proposals.

"The tax increase will not hit us much. We are a multinational company and our sales and profits in France are only a small proportion of the total," said an official and a large insurance company who declined to be indentified.
Analysts said companies with a big exposure to France would be most hit. These are retailers, banks, some food companies and building companies.
Jacques Chahine, of the financial consultancy with the same name, said he expected the higher tax rate would incite companies to tranfer more of their profits abroad.

Another analyst said that by slightly changing internal transfer prices within a company -- lowering the price at which foreign units obtain French products and services and raising the costs of foreign products and services for the parent in France -- companies could reduce their profits in France and increase their foreign earnings.

The effects of a change on the taxation on capital gains are also not straightforward -- while the rate of 41.6 percent is much higher than 19 percent the transfer to the taxable base means they can be offset against one-off costs or recoverable tax losses.
